title: Opinions and Disagreement
overview: Report what people said without taking their side or yours. Turn a question into a reported one, tell a request from an instruction, and choose a reporting verb you could defend if challenged. Then disagree at the right strength, and give reasons, aims and examples in language that belongs in a written record.
learningPath: The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: two records of one meeting, a language guide and a set of minutes.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Write down what somebody asked, without quoting them
Report a request as a request, not as an order
Report somebody fairly, even when you disagree with them
Disagree with somebody senior without causing offence
Say whether something is forbidden or merely optional
Agree to most of a proposal and name what you do not agree to
Give a reason, an aim and an example in formal writing
lectureScript:
This unit is about reporting what other people said, and about disagreeing with them.
Those two things belong together, because the moment you disagree with somebody you have to say what they said first, and how you say it decides everything that follows.

The reading opens with something that really happens in offices.
Two people wrote up the same meeting. One record said the supplier STATED that the part had been faulty. The other said he CLAIMED it.
Nobody changed a single fact. One word did all of it.
Stated is neutral. Claimed tells the reader not to believe him, before they have read anything else.
Hold on to that, because the third pattern in this unit is entirely about it.

The first pattern fills a real gap.
Level 2 showed you how to report a statement and how to report a command.
She said that it was ready. She told me to wait.
It never showed you how to report a QUESTION, and that is the first card.
The trick is one you already own, from Unit 4.
The question goes back into statement order.
Where is the file becomes she asked where the file WAS.
What does it cost becomes he asked what it COST, and the does vanishes.
And if there is no question word, because it was a yes-or-no question, you need whether or if.
Have you finished becomes she asked WHETHER I had finished.
One more thing. There is no question mark. A reported question is a statement about a question, not a question.

The second pattern is a distinction that matters more than it looks.
Level 2 gave you she told me to wait. That reports an instruction, from somebody who could give one.
But if a colleague says could you wait a moment, she ASKED you. She could have been refused.
Reporting that as she told me to wait puts authority in her hands that she did not have.
In ordinary conversation nobody would care. In a complaint, in a grievance, in minutes read by people who were not there, that is the whole difference.
The test is simple. Could the person have said no? If yes, it was a request.
And there is a family of these verbs, each carrying its own force. Warned. Reminded. Urged. Advised. Persuaded.
She warned me not to sign it says there was a danger. She reminded me to sign it says I already knew. Choosing the verb is choosing what you are saying happened.

Which brings us to the third pattern, and this is the one worth the most.
Level 2 treated every reporting verb as neutral. Most of them are not.
Said and stated take no position. Claimed and alleged tell the reader to doubt. Admitted and acknowledged say the speaker gave ground against their own interest. Insisted says they were pushed and did not move. Denied says they rejected it outright.
Before you write a loaded one, ask yourself one question. Can I support this?
If you write claimed about somebody who was telling the truth, you have not reported them. You have accused them, and a reader who knows the facts will notice.
The same runs the other way. Writing she admitted the work was finished is wrong if finishing the work helped her, because admitted means it cost her something.

The fourth pattern is about strength.
You have met most of these modals already, across five cards in Levels 1 and 2, one at a time.
What nobody has done is line them up.
That may not be the whole picture. I might be missing something, but. I am not sure that is right. I do not think that is right. That is not right.
Five ways to say one thing, and they cost you very different amounts.
The skill is picking the softest rung that still says what you mean, because you can always go up and it is very hard to come back down.
There is one pair in here to be careful with, and the reading in this unit is about it.
You must not sign it means signing is forbidden.
You need not sign it means signing is optional.
One word apart, opposite meanings. And the reason it catches people is that must is the exception: with can and should, adding not negates the whole sentence, but must not attacks the action rather than the obligation.

The last pattern gives you four connectives that do work because and so cannot.
As and since give a reason the reader already knows, where because usually gives news.
Therefore gives the result, formally, and it takes a full stop because it is an adverb.
Such as introduces examples, and never needs etc. after it, because such as already means among others.
And so that gives the PURPOSE, which is the one worth slowing down for.
We photographed it so that we had a record means having a record was the aim.
We photographed it, so we had a record means that is what happened to follow.
Both are correct sentences. Only one of them says you were thinking ahead.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

words.meaning: To say something is true, without proving it.
words.example: He claimed the part was faulty when it arrived.
practice: She claims to have sent it twice.
Claim leaves the reader free to doubt it.
Reporting somebody with claim is not neutral.
It is also a noun: an insurance claim.
words.tutor: Report something with claim. Ask the tutor whether it sounded doubtful.

words.meaning: To state something firmly and confidently.
words.example: She asserted that the figures were correct.
practice: He asserted his right to see the file.
Assert is firmer than say and more formal.
Its noun is assertion.
To assert yourself is to stand up for your position.
words.tutor: Report a firm statement with assert. Ask the tutor whether assert or claim was right.

words.meaning: To keep saying something is true, even under challenge.
words.example: He maintained that he had never been told.
practice: She maintains her account has not changed.
Maintain implies the position has been challenged already.
It also means to keep something in good condition.
Its noun for that other meaning is maintenance.
words.tutor: Report somebody holding a position with maintain. Ask the tutor what it implied.

words.meaning: To say something firmly and repeatedly, refusing to give way.
words.example: She insisted that the work was finished.
practice: He insisted on seeing the manager.
Insist takes on before a noun, and that before a clause.
Insisting suggests somebody was pushing back.
Its noun is insistence.
words.tutor: Report somebody refusing to give way. Ask the tutor to check on or that.

words.meaning: To suggest a plan for other people to consider.
words.example: I propose that we meet again in March.
practice: She proposed moving the date.
Propose takes that plus a clause, or an -ing form.
Its noun is proposal.
Propose is formal: in speech you would say suggest.
words.tutor: Make a proposal. Ask the tutor to check the form after propose.

words.meaning: To argue a position, especially against opposition.
words.example: They contend that the fault was there from the start.
practice: Both sides contend the other was at fault.
Contend belongs in a dispute or an argument.
It also means to compete: contending for the place.
Its noun is contention.
words.tutor: Report a disputed position with contend. Ask the tutor whether the dispute came across.

words.meaning: To think something is true.
words.example: I believe the report is accurate.
practice: She believes in doing things properly.
Believe something, but believe IN something you value.
Believe is a state verb: never I am believing.
Its noun is belief.
words.tutor: State a belief. Ask the tutor whether you used believe or believe in correctly.

words.meaning: To think something is probably not true.
words.example: I doubt they will reply before Monday.
practice: There is no doubt about it.
Doubt is followed by whether, or by that in the negative.
It is a state verb, so no -ing form.
No doubt often means probably, not certainly.
words.tutor: Express a doubt. Ask the tutor to check the word after doubt.

words.meaning: Completely certain, usually after being persuaded.
words.example: I am convinced the fault was there already.
practice: She was not convinced by the explanation.
Convinced takes by for the thing that persuaded you.
It is stronger than sure, because somebody persuaded you.
To convince is the verb.
words.tutor: State something you are convinced of. Ask the tutor whether convinced or sure fitted.

words.meaning: Doubting; not easily convinced.
words.example: I am sceptical about the figures.
practice: He was sceptical of the whole plan.
Sceptical takes about or of.
It is spelled with a c in British English.
Being sceptical is not the same as refusing to believe.
words.tutor: Express scepticism. Ask the tutor to check the preposition.

words.meaning: To take something as true without checking.
words.example: I assumed somebody had told her.
practice: Never assume the parts are in stock.
An assumption is where most mistakes begin.
Assume takes that plus a clause.
Its noun is assumption.
words.tutor: Describe an assumption you made. Ask the tutor whether it turned out to be right.

words.meaning: To think something is probably true, without evidence.
words.example: I suspect the seal was already damaged.
practice: She suspected he had not read it.
Suspect is a quiet, cautious form of believe.
The noun is suspicion; the person is a suspect.
Note the stress: the verb is sus-PECT, the noun SUS-pect.
words.tutor: Say what you suspect. Ask the tutor whether you stressed the verb correctly.

words.meaning: To agree, in formal language.
words.example: I concur with the findings.
practice: The two reports concur on every point.
Concur takes with.
It is very formal: minutes, reports, courtrooms.
In speech you would simply say I agree.
words.tutor: Agree formally with concur. Ask the tutor whether the register suited the sentence.

words.meaning: To support something publicly.
words.example: The committee endorsed the proposal.
practice: She would not endorse the plan without figures.
Endorsing is stronger than agreeing: you attach your name.
Its noun is endorsement.
It also means to sign the back of a document.
words.tutor: Report a public endorsement. Ask the tutor how it differed from agreeing.

words.meaning: To agree that something is true or right.
words.example: I accept that the delay was partly ours.
practice: She accepted the explanation without argument.
Accepting a point is conceding it.
Accept takes that plus a clause.
Its noun is acceptance.
words.tutor: Concede a point with accept. Ask the tutor whether the concession cost you anything.

words.meaning: To back a position, or to provide evidence for it.
words.example: The figures support what she said.
practice: I support the proposal, with one reservation.
Evidence supports a claim; people support a plan.
Its noun is support, unchanged.
Supporting evidence is the fixed phrase.
words.tutor: Say what the evidence supports. Ask the tutor which of the two meanings you used.

words.meaning: To admit that something is true, or to say you received it.
words.example: They acknowledged the delay but not the cost.
practice: Please acknowledge receipt of this letter.
Acknowledging is narrower than accepting: you admit only that part.
Its noun is acknowledgement.
Watch the spelling: there is a d before the g.
words.tutor: Report a narrow admission. Ask the tutor to check the spelling.

words.meaning: To hold the same view as somebody else.
words.example: I share her concern about the timing.
practice: We share the same reservations.
Share a view, a concern or a doubt.
It is warmer than agree: you already held the view.
It also has its everyday meaning of dividing something.
words.tutor: Say whose view you share. Ask the tutor whether share or agree was better.

words.meaning: To say that something is not true or not fair.
words.example: They dispute the amount, not the work.
practice: Nobody disputes that the part failed.
Dispute names exactly what you are challenging.
It is also a noun: a dispute over the invoice.
The stress moves: dis-PUTE for the verb.
words.tutor: Dispute one specific thing. Ask the tutor whether you narrowed it enough.

words.meaning: To say you are against something.
words.example: I object to the wording, not the decision.
practice: She objected on the grounds of cost.
Object takes to.
Its noun is objection.
The stress moves: ob-JECT for the verb, OB-ject for the noun.
words.tutor: Object to something specific. Ask the tutor to check you said object TO.

words.meaning: To say the opposite of what somebody else said.
words.example: The second report contradicts the first.
practice: He contradicted himself twice in one letter.
Two accounts contradict each other; a person contradicts somebody.
Its noun is contradiction.
Contradicting is stating the opposite, not disproving it.
words.tutor: Report a contradiction. Ask the tutor whether contradict or dispute was right.

words.meaning: To prove that something is not true.
words.example: The record refutes his account entirely.
practice: You cannot refute a claim by denying it.
Refuting needs evidence; denying does not.
Its noun is refutation.
Many people use refute to mean deny. In careful English it does not.
words.tutor: Refute something with evidence. Ask the tutor whether you had evidence or only a denial.

words.meaning: To hold a different view.
words.example: I disagree with the conclusion.
practice: We disagreed about the timing, not the principle.
Disagree takes with a person, and about a topic.
Its noun is disagreement.
It is the plain, everyday word for all of these.
words.tutor: Disagree, and name what about. Ask the tutor to check with and about.

words.meaning: A doubt that stops you agreeing completely.
words.example: I support it, with one reservation.
practice: She had reservations about the cost.
A reservation is partial: you agree, but not entirely.
It is also a booking: a table reservation.
Without reservation means completely.
words.starter: I support it, with one reservation: …
words.tutor: Agree with one reservation. Ask the tutor whether the reservation was clear.

words.meaning: Something that is true and can be checked.
words.example: The fact is that nobody signed for it.
practice: Check the facts before you write.
A fact can be checked; an opinion cannot.
In fact often introduces a correction.
Its adjective is factual.
words.tutor: State a fact. Ask the tutor whether somebody could check it.

words.meaning: Information that shows whether something is true.
words.example: There is no evidence that it was reported.
practice: The evidence supports her version.
Evidence is uncountable: never an evidence.
A piece of evidence is how you count it.
Evident is the adjective.
words.tutor: Say what there is no evidence for. Ask the tutor to check you did not say an evidence.

words.meaning: Something taken as true without being checked.
words.example: The whole plan rests on one assumption.
practice: That is an assumption, not a fact.
An assumption is invisible until it fails.
It comes from assume.
Making an assumption is not an error; not noticing it is.
words.tutor: Name an assumption behind something. Ask the tutor whether it was ever checked.

words.meaning: A leaning towards one side that stops you judging fairly.
words.example: The survey has an obvious bias.
practice: Everybody has a bias; the question is whether they declare it.
Biased is the adjective, with one s.
Bias takes towards or against.
A biased source is not a useless one.
words.tutor: Name a bias in a source. Ask the tutor whether it made the source useless.

words.meaning: Based on personal feeling rather than on fact.
words.example: That judgement is entirely subjective.
practice: Comfort is subjective; weight is not.
Subjective is the opposite of objective.
A subjective claim is not automatically wrong.
Its noun is subjectivity.
words.tutor: Name something subjective and say why. Ask the tutor whether the reason held.

grammar.title: She asked whether I had finished: reporting a question
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 showed you how to report a STATEMENT and a COMMAND.
She said that it was ready. She told me to wait.
It never showed you how to report a QUESTION, and that is this card.
The trick is one you have already met, in a different place.
grammar.rule:
The question goes back into STATEMENT order, exactly as in a polite question.

Direct:   'Where is the file?'
Reported: She asked where the file WAS.

Direct:   'What does it cost?'
Reported: He asked what it COST.   (does disappears)

A yes-or-no question needs IF or WHETHER:
Direct:   'Have you finished?'
Reported: She asked whether I had finished.

The verb usually steps one tense back:
is -> was      does -> did      have -> had      will -> would

And the pronouns move with the speaker:
'Have YOU finished?' -> She asked whether I had finished.

No question mark, because a reported question is a statement about a question.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Report this: She said, 'What does it cost?'
1. Choose the reporting verb: asked, because it was a question.
2. Keep the question word: what.
3. Put the inside back into statement order: it costs.
4. Step the tense back: costs becomes cost. The does disappears.
5. No question mark: the whole sentence is a statement now.
Answer: She asked what it cost.
grammar.mistake:
Learners keep the question order, exactly as they do with polite questions.
No: She asked where was the file.
Yes: She asked where the file was.
It is the same rule you met with Could you tell me where the venue is.
grammar.tip: A reported question is a statement. Statement order, no question mark.
grammar.practice:
Report each one.
1. She said, 'Where is the file?'
2. He said, 'What does it cost?'
3. She said, 'Have you finished?'
4. He said, 'Did they reply?'
5. She said, 'When will they decide?'
6. He said, 'Who is in charge?'
Now correct these.
7. She asked where was the file.
8. He asked what did it cost?
grammar.answers:
1. She asked where the file was.
2. He asked what it cost.
3. She asked whether I had finished.
4. He asked whether they had replied.
5. She asked when they would decide.
6. He asked who was in charge.
7. She asked where the file was.  8. He asked what it cost. (and no question mark)
Number 6 barely changes, because who was already the subject.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Told me to, or asked me to: the difference is who had the power
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 gave you one of these: she told me to wait.
That reports an instruction from somebody who could give one.
A request is different, and reporting it with tell changes the story.
grammar.rule:
TELL somebody TO do something — an instruction, from somebody with authority.
She told me to wait.
He told them not to sign it.

ASK somebody TO do something — a request, which could have been refused.
She asked me to wait.
He asked them not to sign it.

Both take: verb + person + TO + plain verb.
The negative puts NOT before the to:
She asked me NOT TO sign it.

Neither takes that:
NOT: She asked me that I wait.

Other verbs in the same shape, each carrying its own force:
advised, warned, reminded, persuaded, urged, invited, ordered
She warned me not to sign it.  (a danger)
She reminded me to sign it.    (I already knew)
She urged me to sign it.       (strongly, repeatedly)

Choosing the verb is choosing what you are alleging happened.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Report this, given that she had no authority over you: 'Please wait,' she said.
1. Was it an instruction or a request? A request — she could not order you.
2. A request is reported with ask, not tell.
3. The shape is ask + person + to + plain verb.
Answer: She asked me to wait.
She told me to wait would report her as having authority she did not have.
grammar.mistake:
Reporting a request as an instruction quietly changes who was in charge.
If your colleague says please could you check this, she asked you to check it.
She told me to check it says something different about the relationship,
and in a complaint or a grievance that difference matters.
grammar.tip: tell reports an instruction. ask reports a request. Choose by who could refuse.
grammar.practice:
Report each one with the verb that fits.
1. Your manager: 'Wait here.'
2. A colleague: 'Could you wait a moment?'
3. A friend: 'Whatever you do, do not sign it.' (a danger)
4. Your manager: 'Do not sign it.'
5. A colleague: 'Do not forget to sign it.' (you already knew)
6. A friend, repeatedly: 'You really should apply.'
Now correct these.
7. She asked me that I wait.
8. She asked me to not sign it.
grammar.answers:
1. My manager told me to wait here.
2. A colleague asked me to wait a moment.
3. A friend warned me not to sign it.
4. My manager told me not to sign it.
5. A colleague reminded me to sign it.
6. A friend urged me to apply.
7. She asked me to wait. (ask never takes that in this shape)
8. She asked me not to sign it. (not goes BEFORE to)
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: He claimed, she admitted: the verb that passes judgement
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 treated every reporting verb as neutral: said, told.
Most of them are not. The verb you choose tells the reader what YOU think
of what was said, before they have read a word of it.
In a report or a complaint this is the most loaded choice you make.
grammar.rule:
NEUTRAL — you take no position:
said, stated, told me, explained, mentioned

DOUBTING — you are signalling that it may not be true:
claimed, alleged, maintained
He claimed the part was faulty on arrival.
(the reader now expects it was not)

CONCEDING — the speaker gave ground, against their own interest:
admitted, accepted, acknowledged, conceded
She admitted the invoice had been sent late.

INSISTING — the speaker was pushed and did not move:
insisted, maintained, contended

DENYING — the speaker rejected it:
denied, disputed, rejected
Note: denied takes -ing, not that + to.
He denied sending it. / He denied that he had sent it.

The test before you write one: can you support the judgement?
Writing claimed about somebody who was telling the truth is not neutral reporting.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You are writing a complaint. The supplier said the part was faulty when it
arrived. You have a photograph showing it was not. Which verb?
1. Do you accept what was said? No, and you have evidence.
2. A doubting verb signals that to the reader.
3. claimed is the standard one.
Answer: The supplier claimed the part was faulty on arrival.
Then give the photograph. The verb prepares the reader; the evidence does the work.
grammar.mistake:
A doubting verb with no evidence behind it reads as unfair, and it weakens you.
Weak: He claimed he had posted it. (if you have no reason to doubt him)
Better: He said he had posted it.
Save claimed for when you can show why.
grammar.tip: The verb is your judgement. Only use a loaded one when you can back it.
grammar.practice:
Choose the reporting verb that fits.
1. You have evidence against what he said. He ___ the part was faulty.
2. She gave ground against her own interest. She ___ the invoice was late.
3. You take no position at all. He ___ the office closes at five.
4. He was challenged twice and did not move. He ___ he had never been told.
5. He rejected the accusation outright. He ___ sending it.
6. She agreed to one narrow part only. She ___ the delay, but not the cost.
Now decide whether each is fair.
7. He claimed he had posted it. (you have no reason to doubt him)
8. She admitted the work was finished. (it was, and it helped her)
grammar.answers:
1. claimed  2. admitted (or conceded)  3. said (or stated)
4. maintained (or insisted)  5. denied  6. acknowledged
7. Unfair. Use said. claimed accuses him with nothing behind it.
8. Wrong verb. admitted implies it cost her something, and it did not. Use said or confirmed.
7 and 8 are the judgement the card is teaching.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: May, might, could: disagreeing without a row
grammar.explanation:
You have met most of these modals already, one at a time, across five cards
in Levels 1 and 2. What no card has done is line them up by STRENGTH.
Disagreeing well is almost entirely a matter of picking the right rung.
grammar.rule:
SAYING SOMEBODY IS WRONG, from softest to hardest:
That may not be the whole picture.
I might be missing something, but ...
I am not sure that is right.
I do not think that is right.
That is not right.
All five say the same thing. They cost you very different amounts.

SUGGESTING, softest first:
We could look at it again.
We might want to look at it again.
Perhaps we should look at it again.
We need to look at it again.
We must look at it again.

OBLIGATION AND PROHIBITION, which you already have:
must / have to      an obligation
must not            a prohibition
need not / do not have to   no obligation (NOT a prohibition)

The pair learners confuse, and it matters:
You must not sign it.   = signing is forbidden
You need not sign it.   = signing is optional
Opposite meanings, one word apart.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Your manager states a figure you believe is wrong, in front of other people.
1. Ask what it costs to be blunt here. A lot: it is public, and they are senior.
2. So choose a soft rung, and leave yourself room to be wrong.
3. Add a reason, because a soft disagreement with no reason is just doubt.
Answer: I might be missing something, but I had a different figure for March.
That is not right may be true and buys you nothing you needed.
grammar.mistake:
must not and need not are one word apart and mean opposite things.
You must not sign it = do NOT sign.
You need not sign it = you may sign or not, as you like.
Getting this wrong in writing has real consequences.
grammar.tip: Pick the softest rung that still says what you mean. You can always go up.
grammar.practice:
Choose the best form and be ready to say why.
1. Disagreeing with a senior person in public. I ___ be missing something, but ...
2. Signing is forbidden. You ___ sign it.
3. Signing is optional. You ___ sign it.
4. A gentle suggestion. We ___ look at it again.
5. An obligation you cannot avoid. We ___ look at it again.
6. You are fairly sure but not certain. That ___ not be the whole picture.
Now rewrite each of these more softly.
7. That is wrong.
8. You have to do it again.
grammar.answers:
1. might  2. must not  3. need not  4. could  5. must (or have to)  6. may
7. I am not sure that is right. / That may not be the whole picture.
8. We might want to look at it again. / It could be worth doing again.
Numbers 2 and 3 are the pair that mean opposite things.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: As, therefore, so that, such as: four ways to explain
grammar.explanation:
You have because and so, from Level 1 and Level 2.
Those two cover most of daily speech and almost none of formal writing.
These four each do a job because and so cannot do.
grammar.rule:
AS and SINCE — the reason, given first, when it is already known.
As the part was still under guarantee, we returned it.
Since nobody had signed for it, we could not trace it.
because usually gives NEW information; as and since give known information.

THEREFORE — the result, formally. It is an adverb, so it takes a full stop.
The part was under guarantee. Therefore we returned it.

SO THAT — the PURPOSE, not the result. It answers what for.
We photographed it so that we had a record.
Compare: We photographed it, so we had a record. (that is a result)
so that = in order to. so = and as a result.

SUCH AS — examples, introducing a list you are not finishing.
Several items were missing, such as the seal and the bracket.
like does the same job and is less formal.
Do not use etc. with such as: such as already means among others.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Choose: We photographed it ___ we had a record.
1. Ask what the second half is. Is it what happened, or what you were aiming at?
2. Having a record was the AIM. You photographed it in order to get one.
3. Purpose takes so that.
Answer: We photographed it so that we had a record.
With so alone it would read as a result: we photographed it, and as it turned out,
that gave us a record. True, but not what you meant.
grammar.mistake:
so and so that look almost identical and answer different questions.
so = and as a result (what happened next)
so that = in order that (what you were aiming at)
If you can replace it with in order to, you need so that.
grammar.tip: because gives news. as gives what they already know. so that gives the aim.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right connective.
1. We photographed it ___ we had a record. (that was the aim)
2. It was raining, ___ we stopped. (that is what happened)
3. ___ the part was under guarantee, we returned it. (they know this already)
4. The part was under guarantee. ___ we returned it. (formal, a full stop before it)
5. Several items were missing, ___ the seal and the bracket.
6. ___ nobody had signed for it, we could not trace it.
Now correct these.
7. We kept a copy so we had proof if needed. (you mean the aim)
8. Items were missing, such as the seal, the bracket, etc.
grammar.answers:
1. so that  2. so  3. As  4. Therefore  5. such as  6. Since
7. We kept a copy so that we had proof if needed.
8. Items were missing, such as the seal and the bracket. (such as already means among others)
Numbers 1 and 2 are the pair: the aim, against what happened.
6 or more right: good.

readings.title: Two Versions of the Same Meeting
readings.setting: An office, a week after the meeting
readings.passage:
I wrote the minutes and somebody else wrote a summary, and the two read like different meetings.
Mine said the supplier stated that the part had been faulty on arrival.
The other said the supplier claimed the part had been faulty on arrival.
Nobody changed a single fact. One word did all of it.
Stated is neutral. Claimed tells the reader not to believe him, before they have read anything else.
As it happens, I think he was probably wrong. But we had no evidence either way at that point.
Writing claimed put a judgement into a record that was supposed to hold only what was said.
The second thing I noticed was the requests.
The summary said the manager told the supplier to re-test the batch.
She did not tell him anything. She asked, and he could have said no, and for a while it looked as though he would.
Told makes it an instruction from somebody with authority over him. She had none.
Since the minutes may be read by people who were not there, both of those matter.
A record is not neutral because you meant it to be. It is neutral because you chose the verbs carefully.

readings.title: Must Not and Need Not
readings.setting: A page from a language guide
readings.passage:
Two phrases in English are one word apart and mean opposite things.
You must not sign it means signing is forbidden.
You need not sign it means signing is optional.
The mistake is easy to make and the consequences are not small.
There is a reason it catches people out.
In most pairs, adding not to the modal negates the whole sentence.
You can go becomes you cannot go. You should go becomes you should not go.
But must works differently. Must not negates the ACTION, not the obligation.
The way to remember it is to ask which word the not is attacking.
In you must not sign, the not attacks signing. Signing is what is forbidden.
In you need not sign, the not attacks the need. The need is what is absent.
Do not have to behaves like need not, not like must not.
You do not have to sign means the same as you need not sign.
If you are ever unsure in writing, avoid both and say it plainly.
Signing is not required. Do not sign this form. Neither of those can be misread.

readings.title: Minutes: Supply Review, 14 March
readings.setting: A short set of meeting minutes
readings.passage:
SUPPLY REVIEW — MINUTES
14 March. Present: R. Adeyemi (chair), J. Ferreira, T. Okafor (supplier).

1. T. Okafor stated that the seals had been within specification when despatched.
   He acknowledged that two boxes had been sent without labels.

2. J. Ferreira disputed the specification figures, as the batch record showed a different tolerance.
   T. Okafor maintained that the record referred to an earlier batch.

3. The chair asked whether the batch could be re-tested independently.
   T. Okafor asked for two weeks to arrange this. This was agreed.

4. The chair asked T. Okafor to confirm the arrangements in writing by 21 March,
   so that both parties held the same record.

5. It was agreed that no further orders would be placed until the re-test was complete.
   J. Ferreira noted one reservation: the existing stock need not be returned meanwhile.

Next meeting: 4 April.

comprehension.q: What single word made the two records read differently?
comprehension.why: The writer says nobody changed a fact, and one word did all of it.

comprehension.q: The writer thinks the supplier was probably wrong. Why do they still object to 'claimed'?
comprehension.a: Because there was no evidence either way, and a record should hold only what was said.
comprehension.why: The judgement was not supported at that point, whatever turned out later.

comprehension.q: Why was 'told the supplier to re-test' wrong?
comprehension.a: She asked, and he could have refused. Told reports authority she did not have.
comprehension.why: The text says she had none, and that for a while it looked as though he would refuse.

comprehension.q: What does the writer say makes a record neutral?
comprehension.a: Choosing the verbs carefully, not intending to be fair.
comprehension.why: The last line states it directly.

comprehension.q: What does 'you need not sign it' mean?
comprehension.why: Given in the third line, against must not, which forbids it.

comprehension.q: Why does the article say the mistake is easy to make?
comprehension.a: Because in most modal pairs, adding not negates the whole sentence, and must is an exception.
comprehension.why: The article contrasts can and should with must.

comprehension.q: What does the article suggest if you are unsure in writing?
comprehension.a: Avoid both and say it plainly: signing is not required, or do not sign this form.
comprehension.why: The last two lines, and it says neither can be misread.

comprehension.q: In item 1, which part did the supplier give ground on?
comprehension.a: That two boxes had been sent without labels.
comprehension.why: The verb is acknowledged, which concedes; stated, in the line above, does not.

comprehension.q: In item 4, did the chair instruct or request?
comprehension.a: Requested. The minutes say asked T. Okafor to confirm.
comprehension.why: Asked reports a request; told would have reported an instruction.

comprehension.q: Must the existing stock be returned before the re-test?
comprehension.a: No. The minutes say it need not be returned meanwhile.
comprehension.why: Need not means it is optional, not forbidden.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Report six things somebody said
speaking.instructions:
Report each one aloud. Watch the word order and the tense.
1. She said, 'Where is the file?'
2. He said, 'What does it cost?'
3. She said, 'Have you finished?'
4. Your manager said, 'Wait here.'
5. A colleague said, 'Could you wait a moment?'
6. A friend said, 'Whatever you do, do not sign it.'
Models: She asked where the file was. My manager told me to wait here.
Tap the mic. Report all six. Tap again and listen.
Check: in 1 to 3, did the question go back into statement order?
In 4 to 6, did you choose between told, asked and warned by who had the power?
speaking.tutor: Report the six to the tutor and ask whether any reporting verb changed the story.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — The stress that carries the disagreement
speaking.instructions:
A soft disagreement is soft in the wording and in the voice together.
Say the same words with the stress in two places and hear them change.
Listen and repeat. The capitals show the stress.
I MIGHT be missing something.   (genuinely unsure, and soft)
I might be MISSING something.   (fishing, and it sounds sharper)
That may not be the WHOLE picture.  (there is more — open)
That MAY not be the whole picture.  (I doubt you — pointed)
Now say these three lines twice each, softly and then pointedly.
I am not sure that is right.
Perhaps we should look at it again.
That may not be the whole picture.
Tap the mic. Say each line both ways. Tap again and listen.
Check: can you hear the difference between your two versions?
The words did not change. Only the stress did.
speaking.tutor: Say the three lines both ways and ask the tutor which version sounded more willing to be wrong.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Five rungs on the same disagreement
speaking.instructions:
Somebody has stated a figure you believe is wrong.
Say the same disagreement five times, from softest to hardest.
A model of the ladder:
That may not be the whole picture.
I might be missing something, but I had a different figure.
I am not sure that is right.
I do not think that is right.
That is not right.
Now build your own ladder about something else.
Tap the mic. Say all five of yours, in order. Tap again and listen.
Check: does each one cost you a little more than the last?
Which rung would you actually use with your manager, and which with a friend?
speaking.tutor: Say your five rungs and ask the tutor which one it would use in a meeting with strangers.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Listen: the minutes that were not neutral
speaking.instructions:
Tap Listen. Do not read along. Listen twice.
I wrote the minutes and somebody else wrote a summary of the same meeting.
Mine said the supplier stated that the part had been faulty on arrival.
Theirs said the supplier claimed it.
Nobody changed a fact. One word did all of it.
The summary also said the manager told the supplier to re-test the batch.
She did not tell him anything. She asked, and he could have refused.
For a while it looked as though he would.
Now answer. Tap the mic and say each answer.
1. What were the two records of?
2. Which word did the summary use instead of stated?
3. What does that word tell the reader?
4. Why was told wrong?
Tap again and listen to your answers.
Check: 1 the same meeting. 2 claimed. 3 not to believe him.
4 she asked rather than instructed, and he could have refused.
speaking.tutor: Retell the problem in three sentences and ask which of the two errors was worse.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Agree, with one reservation
speaking.instructions:
For each proposal, agree out loud and then name one reservation.
Use a different agreeing word each time: accept, support, share, acknowledge, concur.
1. Moving the deadline forward by a week.
2. Buying the cheaper parts.
3. Cancelling the second inspection.
4. Asking the supplier to re-test at their own cost.
5. Putting everything in writing from now on.
A model for the first one:
I accept that the date has to move. My one reservation is the testing time.
Tap the mic. Say all five. Tap again and listen.
Check: is each reservation specific enough to act on?
A reservation nobody can address is just a complaint.
speaking.tutor: Say your five and ask the tutor which reservation was clearest.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Two minutes: report a disagreement
speaking.instructions:
Describe a disagreement, real or invented, for two minutes.
Cover these four, in this order:
what each side said, reported
what was asked for, and by whom
what you accept, and what you dispute
what you propose
Keep your reporting verbs fair: only use claimed or denied if you can say why.
Tap the mic. Speak for two minutes without stopping.
Tap again and listen to the whole thing.
Check: did you report any request as an instruction?
Did any reporting verb pass a judgement you could not support?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your two minutes and ask whether you reported the other side fairly.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Report eight things that were said
writing.prompt:
Report each of these. Choose the reporting verb by who had the power and
what you can support.
a) She said, 'Where is the file?'
b) He said, 'What does it cost?'
c) She said, 'Have you finished?'
d) Your manager said, 'Wait here.'
e) A colleague said, 'Could you wait a moment?'
f) A friend said, 'Do not sign it.' (warning you of a danger)
g) He said the part was faulty. You have a photograph showing it was not.
h) She said the invoice was late. It was, and admitting it cost her.
writing.model:
a) She asked where the file was.
b) He asked what it cost.
c) She asked whether I had finished.
d) My manager told me to wait there.
e) A colleague asked me to wait a moment.
f) A friend warned me not to sign it.
g) He claimed the part was faulty.
h) She admitted the invoice had been late.
writing.length: Eight reported sentences, about 70 to 100 words.
writing.criteria:
a, b and c in statement order, with no question marks.
d, e and f each use a different verb, chosen by who had the power.
g uses a doubting verb, because you have evidence.
h uses a conceding verb, because the admission cost her.
writing.support: For d to f, ask first: could the person have said no? If yes, it was a request.
writing.extension: Rewrite (g) as it would read if you had NO photograph, and say what changed.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Minutes that hold only what was said
writing.prompt:
Write five numbered minutes of a meeting you invent, in the style of Reading 3.
Report at least one statement, one concession, one dispute and one request.
Use only reporting verbs you could defend if somebody challenged them.
writing.model:
1. T. Okafor stated that the seals had been within specification when despatched.
   He acknowledged that two boxes had been sent without labels.
2. J. Ferreira disputed the figures, as the batch record showed a different tolerance.
3. The chair asked whether the batch could be re-tested independently.
4. The chair asked T. Okafor to confirm the arrangements in writing by 21 March.
5. It was agreed that no further orders would be placed until the re-test was complete.
writing.length: Five numbered items, about 90 to 130 words.
writing.criteria:
At least four different reporting verbs, each defensible.
Every request reported with ask, not tell, unless authority is clear.
At least one reported question, in statement order.
No opinion of your own anywhere in the minutes.
writing.support: Write what each person actually said in quotation marks first, then convert it.
writing.extension: Rewrite item 1 using claimed instead of stated, and write one sentence on what changed for the reader.

writing.title: Writing 3 — The same disagreement, five ways
writing.prompt:
Somebody has stated something you believe is wrong.
Write the disagreement five times, from softest to hardest, and then say
in one sentence which you would send and why.
Invent the situation.
writing.model:
That may not be the whole picture.
I might be missing something, but I had a different figure for March.
I am not sure that is right.
I do not think that figure is right.
That figure is not right.

I would send the second, because it gives a reason and still lets me be wrong.
writing.length: Five versions plus one sentence, about 70 to 100 words.
writing.criteria:
Five clearly different strengths, in order.
At least two use a modal: may, might, could.
At least one gives a reason as well as a position.
The final sentence names the audience, not just the wording.
writing.support: Write the hardest version first, then soften it one step at a time.
writing.extension: Write the version you would use if you had already been proved right once that day.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Explain it four ways
writing.prompt:
Write six sentences about one incident, using as, since, therefore,
so that and such as. Each connective at least once.
Then write one sentence explaining the difference between your so and your so that.
writing.model:
As the part was still under guarantee, we returned it the same day.
Since nobody had signed for the delivery, we could not trace it.
The seal was missing. Therefore the whole batch had to be quarantined.
We photographed everything so that we had a record of the condition.
Several items were missing, such as the seal and the mounting bracket.
It was raining, so we stopped for the afternoon.

so that gave the aim of photographing; so gave what happened because of the rain.
writing.length: Six sentences plus one, about 90 to 120 words.
writing.criteria:
as, since, therefore, so that and such as each used at least once.
therefore follows a full stop, not a comma.
so that introduces an aim; so introduces a result.
No etc. after such as.
writing.support: For each sentence, ask whether you are giving a reason, a result, an aim or an example.
writing.extension: Rewrite the so that sentence using in order to, and say which you prefer.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Report the question
activities.instructions:
Report each one. Watch the word order, the tense and the punctuation.
1. She said, 'Where is the file?'
2. He said, 'What does it cost?'
3. She said, 'Have you finished?'
4. He said, 'Did they reply?'
5. She said, 'When will they decide?'
6. He said, 'Who is in charge?'
7. She said, 'Why did nobody tell me?'
Now correct these.
8. She asked where was the file.
9. He asked what did it cost?
activities.answers:
1. She asked where the file was.  2. He asked what it cost.
3. She asked whether I had finished.  4. He asked whether they had replied.
5. She asked when they would decide.  6. He asked who was in charge.
7. She asked why nobody had told her.
8. She asked where the file was.  9. He asked what it cost. (no question mark)
Number 6 hardly changes, because who was already the subject of its clause.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Say each one aloud before writing. The wrong order sounds wrong before it looks wrong.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Told, asked, warned or reminded?
activities.instructions:
Report each one with the verb that fits who had the power and what was meant.
1. Your manager: 'Wait here.'
2. A colleague: 'Could you wait a moment?'
3. A friend: 'Whatever you do, do not sign it.' (a danger)
4. Your manager: 'Do not sign it.'
5. A colleague: 'Do not forget to sign it.' (you already knew)
6. A friend, repeatedly: 'You really should apply.'
7. A stranger: 'Would you mind moving your bag?'
Now correct these.
8. She asked me that I wait.
9. She asked me to not sign it.
activities.answers:
1. told me to wait  2. asked me to wait  3. warned me not to sign it
4. told me not to sign it  5. reminded me to sign it  6. urged me to apply
7. asked me to move my bag
8. She asked me to wait.  9. She asked me not to sign it. (not goes before to)
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For each one ask: could the speaker have been refused? If yes, it was a request.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Choose the verb, then defend it
activities.instructions:
Choose the reporting verb, and write in three words why.
1. You have evidence against what he said. He ___ the part was faulty.
2. She gave ground against her own interest. She ___ the invoice was late.
3. You take no position. He ___ the office closes at five.
4. He was challenged twice and did not move. He ___ he had never been told.
5. He rejected the accusation outright. He ___ sending it.
6. She agreed to one narrow part. She ___ the delay, but not the cost.
Now judge these two.
7. He claimed he had posted it. (you have no reason to doubt him)
8. She admitted the work was finished. (it was, and it helped her)
activities.answers:
1. claimed — you doubt it  2. admitted — against interest  3. said — neutral
4. maintained — held under pressure  5. denied — outright rejection
6. acknowledged — narrow concession
7. Unfair. Use said. claimed accuses him with nothing behind it.
8. Wrong. admitted implies it cost her, and it did not. Use said or confirmed.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the verb, then the three-word reason. If you cannot write the reason, the verb is wrong.

activities.title: Practice 4 — The ladder
activities.instructions:
Choose the right form.
1. Disagreeing with a senior person in public. I ___ be missing something.
2. Signing is forbidden. You ___ sign it.
3. Signing is optional. You ___ sign it.
4. A gentle suggestion. We ___ look at it again.
5. An obligation you cannot avoid. We ___ look at it again.
6. Fairly sure, not certain. That ___ not be the whole picture.
Now rewrite each of these more softly.
7. That is wrong.
8. You have to do it again.
9. You must not leave before five.  (make it optional instead)
activities.answers:
1. might  2. must not  3. need not  4. could  5. must (or have to)  6. may
7. I am not sure that is right.
8. We might want to look at it again.
9. You need not leave before five. (or: you do not have to)
Numbers 2, 3 and 9 turn on the pair that means opposite things one word apart.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Say each softened version aloud. If it still sounds blunt, the wording is not the problem.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Reason, result, aim or example?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right connective.
1. We photographed it ___ we had a record. (that was the aim)
2. It was raining, ___ we stopped. (that is what happened)
3. ___ the part was under guarantee, we returned it. (they know this already)
4. The part was under guarantee. ___ we returned it. (formal)
5. Several items were missing, ___ the seal and the bracket.
6. ___ nobody had signed for it, we could not trace it.
7. We kept a copy ___ we had proof. (the aim)
Now correct these.
8. Items were missing, such as the seal, the bracket, etc.
9. It was raining, therefore we stopped.
activities.answers:
1. so that  2. so  3. As  4. Therefore  5. such as  6. Since  7. so that
8. ... such as the seal and the bracket. (such as already means among others)
9. It was raining. Therefore we stopped. (therefore is an adverb and needs a full stop)
Numbers 1 and 2 are the pair: the aim, against what happened.
7 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For each, ask which question you are answering: why, what happened, what for, or like what?

activities.title: Practice 6 — Take the judgement out
activities.instructions:
Each line is from a record that was meant to be neutral. Rewrite it so it is.
1. The supplier claimed the part had been faulty on arrival.
2. The manager told the supplier to re-test the batch. (she asked; she had no authority)
3. He admitted the office closes at five.
4. She alleged that the invoice had been sent on the third.
5. The contractor insisted the site had been cleared. (nobody had challenged him)
activities.answers:
1. The supplier stated that the part had been faulty on arrival.
2. The manager asked the supplier to re-test the batch.
3. He said the office closes at five. (admitted implies it cost him something)
4. She stated that the invoice had been sent on the third.
5. The contractor said the site had been cleared. (insisted implies he was pushed)
Every one of these loads a record with a judgement the writer could not support.
4 or 5 right: good.
activities.solo: For each one, write what the loaded verb implied. Then write the version that implies nothing.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the minutes
activities.instructions:
Answer from Reading 3 only.
1. Who chaired the meeting?
2. What did T. Okafor acknowledge?
3. What did J. Ferreira dispute, and on what grounds?
4. Copy the reported question and say how you know it is one.
5. Copy the request in item 4 and say why ask is the right verb.
6. Does the existing stock have to be returned? Quote the words that tell you.
activities.answers:
1. R. Adeyemi.
2. That two boxes had been sent without labels.
3. The specification figures, because the batch record showed a different tolerance.
4. 'The chair asked whether the batch could be re-tested independently.'
   It is in statement order, uses whether, and has no question mark.
5. 'The chair asked T. Okafor to confirm the arrangements in writing.'
   ask reports a request that could have been refused; told would claim authority.
6. No. 'the existing stock need not be returned meanwhile' — need not means optional.
5 or 6 right: good.
activities.solo: Read the minutes with a pen and circle every reporting verb before you answer.

quizzes.q: She said, 'Where is the file?' Reported: She asked where the file ___ .
quizzes.why: The verb steps one tense back, and the question goes into statement order, so the file comes before was.

options: He asked what did it cost.
He asked what does it cost?
quizzes.why: A reported question is a statement: statement order, no does, and no question mark.

quizzes.q: She said, 'Have you finished?' Reported: She asked ___ I had finished.
quizzes.why: A yes-or-no question has no question word, so whether or if joins the clause on.

quizzes.q: A colleague with no authority over you says 'Could you wait?' How is that reported?
options: She asked me that I wait.
quizzes.why: She could have been refused, so it was a request. told would report authority she did not have.
In this shape the not comes before the to, never between to and the verb.

quizzes.q: You have a photograph showing the part was fine. How do you report what he said?
options: He said the part was faulty.
He claimed the part was faulty.
He admitted the part was faulty.
He acknowledged the part was faulty.
quizzes.a: He claimed the part was faulty.
quizzes.why: claimed signals doubt, and you can support the doubt. admitted and acknowledged would mean he conceded something, which he did not.

quizzes.q: You have no reason at all to doubt him. Which is fair?
options: He claimed he had posted it.
He alleged he had posted it.
He said he had posted it.
He insisted he had posted it.
quizzes.a: He said he had posted it.
quizzes.why: The other three each accuse him of something. A loaded verb you cannot back reads as unfair and weakens you.

quizzes.q: Signing is optional. You ___ sign it.
quizzes.why: need not removes the obligation. must not forbids the action, which is the opposite, and it is one word away.

quizzes.q: You are disagreeing with a senior person in front of others. Which is best?
options: I might be missing something, but I had a different figure.
I do not think that is right.
quizzes.a: I might be missing something, but I had a different figure.
quizzes.why: It gives a reason and leaves you room to be wrong, which is what a public disagreement with a senior person needs.

quizzes.q: We photographed it ___ we had a record. (having a record was the aim)
quizzes.why: so that gives the purpose; so alone would report it as a result that happened to follow.

quizzes.q: ___ the part was under guarantee, we returned it. (everybody already knew this)
quizzes.why: as and since give a reason the reader already knows. because usually introduces new information.

options: It was raining, therefore we stopped.
It was raining therefore, we stopped.
It was raining, therefore, we stopped.
It was raining. Therefore we stopped.
quizzes.a: It was raining. Therefore we stopped.
quizzes.why: therefore is an adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot hold two complete sentences together with a comma.

teacherNotes.note: Reported speech is placed twice in Level 3: 7Ug.10 here and 8Ug.12 in Unit 9. This unit takes reported questions and the reporting verb; Unit 9 takes the full backshift into the past perfect, which needs 8Ug.08 and cannot be taught at Stage 7. Do not let this unit teach the past perfect.

L2 U17 taught reported statements, reported commands, say against tell, and the time-word shifts. None of that is repeated. The five modal cards in L1 U4 and U18 and L2 U7, U10 and U19 all teach what each modal MEANS; card 4 here is the first to compare their strength.

Reported question word order fails for the same reason indirect questions do in Unit 4, and a learner who got one wrong will get the other wrong. Teach them as the same rule: only the outside is a question.

must not and need not are one word apart and mean opposite things. Reading 2 explains why the error happens, which is worth more than drilling it: must is the exception among the modals, and learners generalise correctly from can and should.

Card 3 teaches learners to notice loaded reporting verbs. Practice 6 asks them to remove judgements from a record. The lesson is fairness in both directions: item 8 in Pattern 3's practice marks a CONCEDING verb as unfair too, so the class does not conclude that only doubting verbs are loaded.

Several words here (concur, contend, endorse, refute) belong to minutes and reports and would sound odd in conversation. The practice lines say so word by word. Note also that refute means to disprove, not to deny, and that many native speakers use it wrongly; the entry says this rather than pretending the usage is settled.
Writing 2 is the unit's real assessment: minutes that hold only what was said. It is marked on whether every reporting verb is defensible, not on vocabulary range.

selfAssessment.statement: I can report a question in statement order, with no question mark.
I know to use whether or if when there is no question word.
I can tell a request from an instruction, and report each correctly.
I can choose a reporting verb I could defend if somebody challenged it.
I can spot when somebody else's reporting verb is passing judgement.
I can disagree at five different strengths, and pick the right one.
I know that must not forbids and need not releases.
I can tell so that from so: the aim, against what happened.

assignment.title: Minutes, and then the disagreement
assignment.instructions:
Part one. Write five numbered minutes of a meeting you invent, in about 130 words.
Include at least one reported question, one request, one concession and one dispute.
Use at least five different reporting verbs, and beside each one, in brackets, write
three words saying why that verb is defensible.
Part two. You disagree with one thing decided in that meeting.
Write the disagreement five times, softest to hardest, then say which you would send
and to whom.
Part three. Write four sentences about the same incident using as, therefore, so that
and such as, each once.
Nothing in part one may contain an opinion of your own.
assignment.submissionType: Written minutes, a disagreement ladder and four linked sentences
